answer: A rule at my workplace that I genuinely agree with is the policy of allowing flexible working hours. I work at an education consultancy, where the workload goes up and down with application deadlines, so this rule makes a real difference. Rather than forcing everyone to arrive at a fixed time, we are allowed to start and finish within a reasonable window. This rule exists because the company recognises that people work best at different times and have different personal commitments. One of my colleagues, for example, drops her children at school every morning, and another prefers to start early and leave before evening. What I appreciate is that it treats employees as responsible adults, rather than having them constantly [[micromanaged]]. People follow it responsibly, ensuring their work still gets done, and in my experience it has made everyone more productive. We simply agree on core hours for meetings and keep each other updated. I agree with it strongly because it has noticeably improved [[morale]] and reduced unnecessary stress, such as sitting in rush-hour traffic. Honestly, I think it is a genuinely [[progressive]] and sensible approach. It has made me far more loyal to the company, and I think it helps us keep good staff, who might otherwise be tempted by bigger firms in Dhaka. I believe rules like this, which trust employees and prioritise results over [[rigid]] attendance, are the future of work. They create a healthier and more balanced working environment for everyone, and I think other employers would be wise to [[follow suit]].

followUps.q: Has anyone ever taken advantage of this rule?
followUps.answer: Once or twice, someone started arriving very late and missing meetings. Our manager had a quiet word with them, and it was sorted out quickly. On the whole, people respect the trust they are given.

followUps.q: Is there a rule at work you disagree with?
followUps.answer: Not strongly, but I find the dress code a little formal for days when we don't meet clients. Still, I understand why it exists, since first impressions matter in our line of work.

note: Set it at his education consultancy, added colleague examples and how the rule works in practice; moved plain marks (productive, sensible, balanced) to [[micromanaged]], [[morale]], [[rigid]], [[follow suit]].
